concept.name: Backspread
concept.definition: A backspread is a vertical-style spread in which more options are bought than sold at different strikes, same type and expiration — for example, short one call at a lower strike and long two calls at a higher strike. It is the converse of the ratio spread: the CFTC glossary describes it as a delta-neutral ratio spread in which more options are bought than sold, benefiting from an increase in volatility.
concept.intuition: You sell one near option to finance two further-out options, creating a position that loses a little in a quiet market but pays off disproportionately in a large directional move.
concept.mechanics: Common structure is 1 short x 2 long, often entered near zero net cost. A call backspread has unlimited upside gain beyond the long strikes and a bounded maximum loss when the underlying pins the long strike at expiration; put backspreads mirror this to the downside. The position is net long vega and long gamma.
concept.formula: 1x2 call backspread payoff = 2 x max(S_T - K2, 0) - max(S_T - K1, 0) + net credit; max loss at S_T = K2 equals (K2 - K1) - net credit.
concept.failure_modes: The maximum loss sits exactly at the long strike — the price level traders instinctively anchor to — and slow grind moves lose to time decay; gains require a fast, large move, since a late move arrives after the short leg has already hurt.
concept.misconceptions: A backspread is not 'unlimited profit for free': the zero or credit entry embeds a real loss zone between the strikes, and the position loses in the most common (quiet) scenarios.
concept.example: With XYZ at $100, sell one $100 call for $4.00 and buy two $105 calls for $2.00 each (zero cost). Max loss $500 if XYZ finishes at $105; above $110 the two long calls outrun the short and profit grows without bound.

citations.source: CFTC Glossary — A Guide to the Language of the Futures Industry
